product: Ponder, a screenless AI tutor desk unit
brief: A screenless desk tutor for kids 6 to 14: it sees the homework through a downward camera, hears through microphones and talks through a speaker; the thinking happens in the cloud.
summary: A document camera crossed with an AIY-style voice kit. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W sits in a small head pod with a Camera Module 3 Wide looking down at the page, two I2S MEMS microphones and a MAX98357A I2S amp (the Google AIY Voice HAT v1 audio design, built from breakouts). The head hangs from a 15 in hollow lamp gooseneck that leaves the base pointing up and turns down into the head's top; only a 10-wire ribbon runs through it (power up, speaker and two signals down). A two-part printed base holds the 40 mm speaker, the talk button, an 8-LED status bar, the USB-C input and 425 g of bought steel discs clamped to the arm's threaded pipe. A DPDT toggle on the head cuts the microphones' data line and supply. A printed shutter covers the lens. No custom PCB.
architecture: Power: Raspberry Pi 15 W USB-C supply (5.1 V, 3 A) -> USB-C breakout in the base (5.1 k CC resistors) -> 120 mm of 22 AWG to the base junction protoboard -> 3 x 5 V + 3 x GND conductors up the arm -> the bonnet's 5 V rail, pins 2/4 (back-powering the Pi through the header)
Base 5 V also feeds: NeoPixel stick through a 1N4001 diode (drops VDD to about 4.3 V so 3.3 V data is a valid high), and the talk button's green LED through 220 ohm
Compute: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W with header, in the head, on a Perma-Proto Bonnet Mini that carries all head wiring

Camera: Camera Module 3 Wide (IMX708, 102 x 67 deg) -> 38 mm Standard-Mini FPC (15-pin 1 mm to 22-pin 0.5 mm, from the official Zero case kit) -> Zero 2 W CSI connector; sensor's long side along the page's long side; fixed lens position set on the first unit
I2S bus (Pi is master, googlevoicehat-soundcard overlay, 48 kHz): BCLK GPIO18 (pin 12), LRCLK GPIO19 (pin 35), DIN GPIO20 (pin 38) from the mics, DOUT GPIO21 (pin 40) to the amp
Mics: 2 x SPH0645 breakouts share BCLK/LRCLK (through 1 k series resistors) and one DOUT line; left mic SEL to GND, right mic SEL to the switched mic supply

Amp: MAX98357A breakout in the head, VIN from 5 V, SD_MODE on GPIO16 (pin 36, as on the AIY Voice HAT), which selects the left channel, so the client plays mono; software caps it at 2.5 W; speaker pair runs down the arm to the 40 mm 4 ohm speaker in the base

Mute (hardware): DPDT toggle on the head. Pole 1: COM = Pi 3V3, throw A = mic VDD, throw B = red LED + GPIO24 (pin 18) sense. Pole 2: COM = GPIO20, throw A = mic DOUT, throw B = GND. Muted = the mic data line open and GPIO20 grounded (this is what makes it real), and the mic supply disconnected (left floating)

Camera-on light: green LED + two 220 ohm in parallel (about 10 mA) on GPIO25 (pin 22), lit by software whenever the camera is streaming (software only, by choice); the printed lens shutter in the head is the hardware camera-off
Status light: NeoPixel stick (8 x 5050) in the base on SPI0 MOSI GPIO10 (pin 19) with core_freq=250, data wire down the arm to 440 ohm (2 x 220) at DIN; SPI keeps it off the I2S pins
Talk button: 16 mm momentary on the base top, GPIO23 (pin 16, AIY convention) to GND with internal pull-up, debounced in software, wire down the arm
Arm harness (10 x 28 AWG silicone ribbon, 690 mm): 1-3 5V, 4 GND, 5 SPK+, 6 SPK-, 7 GND, 8 LED data, 9 GND, 10 BTN; runs through head nipple, coupling, gooseneck, coupling, base nipple

Mechanical stack at the arm root: coupling in a seat on a 2 mm collar on the base top -> 1-3/4 in 1/8 IPS nipple, 8 mm into the coupling, down through the top shell, a printed column and two 3 in steel discs -> hex nut under the discs, discs on 8 mm floor ribs; the pipe end stays 3.9 mm above the harness groove floor so the wires can turn out

assembly: First article. Order A (order-a.csv) buys parts for 2 units. Build both with these steps, then check every item below and write what you measure into design.json; rerun `distinta cad ponder` and `distinta all ponder`, and place order B (order-b.csv) only when every item passes. Gooseneck: hollow, male 1/8 IPS thread at both ends, mass (320 g assumed), the rigid threaded length at each end (12.7 mm assumed) and the tightest bend it holds (40 mm radius assumed). Bore: the 10-wire harness pulls through the gooseneck and both nipples by hand (it needs about 6 mm). Nipple thread OD (10.29 mm assumed): it passes the 11 mm arm holes without forcing. Base stack: with the nipple 8 mm into the coupling and the nut tight, its lower end is at least 3.4 mm above the groove floor and the gooseneck still gets 5 mm or more of thread in that coupling. Head: the camera's holes sit on the four pins, the lens clears the closed shutter, the 38 mm cable reaches both connectors without strain, the toggle body (13.2 x 13.2 mm assumed) clears the camera with the head closed, the SD card goes in and out, the mic sound holes are centred on the ports, and the M2.5 screws clamp the Pi without bottoming. Base: the junction board drops onto its posts, the USB-C socket is centred in the back-wall opening, the speaker (18.3 mm tall) sits in its ring, and the feet fit their 8.4 x 2 mm pockets. Inserts: an M3 screw tightened into an insert in a 4.0 mm hole does not spin it. Kits: the bonnet kit's 2x20 header is female (it must press onto the Pi's male header) and the Seeed Basic Kit contents are listed; if the kit includes an SD card or a supply, drop that line from order B. Electrical, from the test sheet (step 34): 5 V at the bonnet stays at 4.75 V or more, the USB-C meter reads 2.6 A or less, and `vcgencmd get_throttled` reads 0x0. Wi-Fi: with the head closed, `iw dev wlan0 link` reads no more than about 10 dB below a bare Zero 2 W in the same spot. Mechanical: the drop and tip tests in step 35 pass.

Tools: soldering iron with a fine tip plus M3 and M2.5 heat-set insert tips; multimeter with a continuity beeper; USB-C power meter; digital calipers; a 1 g kitchen scale; drill bits or pin gauges from 5 to 8 mm to gauge the bore; flush cutters; wire strippers for 22 to 28 AWG; Phillips #0 and #1 screwdrivers; a 5/8 in wrench for the nuts; soft-jaw pliers or a strap wrench for the round couplings; a deburring tool for the nipple ends; a 0.5 mm steel pull wire or fish tape at least 500 mm long; tweezers; a PCB holder; a set square; a luggage scale for the tip test; a hot-glue gun; a heat gun; a computer with Raspberry Pi Imager and a microSD reader.

Consumables for 20 units (not in the order list or the total): lead-free solder 0.5 to 0.8 mm (about 50 g) and a flux pen; hot-glue sticks (about 20); medium-strength threadlocker such as Loctite 243 (10 ml); polyimide (Kapton) tape 12 to 20 mm wide (1 roll); heat-shrink assortment 1.5 to 6 mm; 1 mm double-sided foam tape (1 roll); paper tape for tape flags; a white paint marker; isopropyl alcohol.

Before building, ask the school's IT staff: is there a 2.4 GHz network the Pi can join (the Zero 2 W has no 5 GHz), is it WPA2-Personal or WPA2-Enterprise, must devices be registered by MAC address, and can the Ponder backend host be allowlisted. The unit test sheet needs the answer.

Golden SD card, step 1 of 4. In Raspberry Pi Imager pick Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W and Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). In the settings set hostname ponder-00, a user, your SSH key and Wi-Fi country US, and the school network if it is WPA2-Personal. Write and verify, then edit config.txt on the card's boot partition: add `dtoverlay=googlevoicehat-soundcard`, `dtparam=spi=on` and `core_freq=250` (the Zero 2 W has the Pi 3's SoC, whose SPI clock follows the core clock and would upset the NeoPixel timing), and comment out `dtparam=audio=on` so the voice card is the only sound card.

Golden SD card, step 2 of 4. Boot it in the first unit's Pi (or any Zero 2 W) and run `sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y sox python3-picamera2 python3-venv rpicam-apps-lite`, then make a venv at /opt/ponder/venv and `pip install adafruit-circuitpython-neopixel-spi` in it. Find the voice card's name with `aplay -l`. Write /etc/asound.conf so the default device is that card by name, played through a softvol control with `max_dB -1.1` (caps the amp at 2.5 W of its 3.2 W) and recorded straight from the card. If the school uses WPA2-Enterprise, add the network now with `nmcli` (802-1x settings from IT).

Golden SD card, step 3 of 4: keep frames and audio off the card. Turn off any swap file or partition on the SD card (`swapon --show` may list zram only), set `Storage=volatile` in /etc/systemd/journald.conf, and make /tmp a tmpfs (`findmnt /tmp` shows tmpfs). The overlay file system goes on per unit, last (step 33).

Golden SD card, step 4 of 4: the client. The Ponder device client is not written yet (the B0tes/ponder-tutor repo holds the web app only). When it exists, install it from a tagged release into /opt/ponder as a systemd service that reads the backend URL and a per-unit token from /etc/ponder/device.conf. It must: debounce GPIO23 (push-to-talk) in software, read mute from GPIO24, turn on GPIO25 before it starts the camera and off after it stops, drive the light bar on SPI at no more than 50 % brightness, play mono (the amp plays the left channel only), hold the camera at a fixed lens position (3.6 dioptres to start, set on the first unit), never use a Bluetooth headset's microphone (the hardware mute covers the built-in mics only), and keep frames and audio in RAM. Then shut down, copy the card to an image file with Imager or `dd`, and write that image to all 21 cards. Label each card with a unit number.

Check the prints. Base top, base bottom, head upper, head lower and shutter are PA12 (MJF, grey as printed); the diffuser is natural PETG. Clear loose powder out of holes and slots. The shutter should slide its full 18 mm in the head lower's track with its thumb nub through the floor slot.
Press in the heat-set inserts with the iron at about 220 C, square and flush: 6 x M3 in the base top bosses, 4 x M3 in the head upper bosses, 4 x M2.5 in the head lower's Pi posts.

Harness: cut 690 mm of the 10-wire ribbon. It is all black, so count from one edge and put a numbered tape flag on wire 1 and wire 10 at both ends, and a HEAD flag on one end. Order: 1-3 5V, 4 GND, 5 SPK+, 6 SPK-, 7 GND, 8 LED data, 9 GND, 10 BTN. Beep every wire end to end with the meter. Peel the wires apart along the middle, keeping 30 mm joined at each end so the order stays and the bundle goes round through the pipe.

Bonnet: solder the 2x20 header that comes with the Perma Proto Bonnet Mini onto it. All head wiring goes on the bonnet. Signal jumpers are single wires peeled from the rest of the two ribbons, cut 120 mm so the shells can lie side by side, with a tape flag naming each end. Use 22 AWG from the hook-up set for the amp's VIN and GND, in two colours kept the same on every unit.

Mics: put a 1 k resistor in the BCLK line from GPIO18 (pin 12) and one in the LRCLK line from GPIO19 (pin 35); both mics share these two lines after the resistors. Each mic's GND goes to GND. Join both mics' 3V pins into one wire (mic VDD) and both DOUT pins into another (mic DATA); both go to the toggle. Tie the left mic's SEL to GND and the right mic's SEL to mic VDD.

Mute toggle: pole 1 COM to 3V3, throw A to mic VDD, throw B to GPIO24 (pin 18) and, through 220 ohm, to the red LED's anode; red LED cathode to GND. Pole 2 COM to GPIO20 (pin 38), throw A to mic DATA, throw B to GND. Sleeve every lug in heat-shrink. With the meter, find the lever position that joins COM to throw B: that is MUTE.

Amp: VIN to 5V and GND to GND (22 AWG), BCLK to GPIO18 and LRC to GPIO19 (straight from the Pi pins, not through the 1 k resistors), DIN to GPIO21 (pin 40), SD to GPIO16 (pin 36). Leave its terminal block off; the speaker pair solders to its + and - pads later. Camera light: GPIO25 (pin 22) through two 220 ohm in parallel to the green LED's anode, cathode to GND. Heat-shrink the LED legs and in-line resistors.

Head upper, before the arm goes on: push the green LED into the front hole nearer the camera end and the red LED into the other one, from inside, and fix them with hot glue. Mount the toggle in the end-wall hole with its nut so the lever points down at the engraved MUTE in the MUTE position. Seat each mic in its pocket with its sound hole over the shell's port, and run hot glue round the board edge without covering the port.

Arm: deburr the inside of both nipple ends. Mark the 1-3/4 in nipple 8 mm from one end with the paint marker. Screw the 1/2 in nipple through the head upper's top hole with a nut inside and a coupling outside, and tighten. Screw the gooseneck into that coupling, the second coupling onto its lower end, and the marked end of the 1-3/4 in nipple into the second coupling up to the mark. A drop of threadlocker on every thread. Before it sets, turn the head so its long side is parallel to the base's front edge when the arm is in the pose of step 32 (check against a square).

Pull the harness through with the pull wire: BASE end in from inside the head upper, through the head nipple, the gooseneck and out of the bottom of the 1-3/4 in nipple. Leave 130 mm inside the head and the rest out of the bottom. Slide a 25 mm piece of 6 mm heat-shrink over the bundle where it will leave the base nipple, and shrink it.

Solder the harness HEAD end to the bonnet: wires 1-3 to the 5V rail (pins 2 and 4), wires 4, 7 and 9 to GND, 5 and 6 (SPK+, SPK-) to the amp's speaker pads, 8 (LED) to GPIO10 (pin 19), 10 (BTN) to GPIO23 (pin 16).
Head lower: drop the shutter into the camera end of its track (the end without lips), thumb nub down through the floor slot, and slide it over the window. It has to go in before the camera.

Camera: plug the wide (15-pin) end of the 38 mm Standard-Mini cable into the camera, contacts toward the camera board. Seat the camera lens-down on the four pins with the cable edge toward the Pi end, and hold it with a small dab of hot glue on each of the four pins. Check the shutter still slides under it.

Pi: push the SD card in first (it can't go in once the Pi is mounted, because the end wall is 2.5 mm away). Plug the narrow (22-pin) end of the camera cable into the Pi's camera connector, contacts toward the board, and close the latch. Screw the Pi to the four M2.5 inserts with M2.5 x 6 screws, SD end toward the end away from the camera. The cable makes one short loop between the two connectors; don't crease it.

Base top, upside down: fit the talk button through its hole with the ring nut inside. Press the speaker into the ring under the grille, cone toward the grille, and run hot glue round its rim. Glue the diffuser into the light-bar slot from inside (flange against the top skin), lay the NeoPixel stick in its frame behind it with the LEDs toward the diffuser, and run hot glue along both long edges of the stick onto the frame rails so it can't drop when the base is turned over.

Arm root: from the outside, push the 1-3/4 in nipple through the base top's arm hole and column until the coupling sits in its seat on the collar. Cover the top face of one steel disc with Kapton, leaving the centre hole clear. Thread the harness tail through that disc (Kapton face toward the shell), then the second disc, then a nut, and let them hang on the wires for now.

Junction board (quarter Perma-Proto): bring in USB-C VBUS and GND from the breakout on 120 mm of 22 AWG each (the two power colours), with a strain-relief loop at the breakout, and the harness's 5V (1-3) and GND (4, 7, 9). From 5V, the 1N4001 (stripe toward the stick) to the stick's 5V, and 220 ohm to the talk button's LED anode. GND to the stick's GND, the button LED's cathode and one button leg. Harness LED wire (8) through two 220 ohm in series to the stick's DIN, as close to the stick as the wire allows; BTN (10) to the other button leg; SPK+ and SPK- (5, 6) to the speaker. Trim every lead flush on the solder side and cover that side with Kapton.

Press the junction board onto its two posts and heat-stake the pins: touch each pin tip with the flat of the iron until it mushrooms over the hole. Then slide the discs and the nut up the wires onto the nipple and run the nut up tight with the wrench, so coupling, shell, column and discs clamp together; hold the gooseneck with the strap wrench so it doesn't twist. The Kapton face of the top disc now sits about 2.8 mm under the board's Kapton-covered solder side.

Set the USB-C breakout in the cradle on the bottom plate with its socket in the back-wall opening and fix it with hot glue on the cradle walls, so plugging in can't move it. Lay the harness tail in the groove under the nipple and out through the gap in the disc ring.

Before first power, with the bonnet unplugged from the Pi and no supply connected, beep with the meter: harness 5V to GND at the bonnet is not a short (the reading climbs as the capacitors charge); the BTN and LED wires show no continuity to 5V; BTN shows continuity to GND only while the talk button is held; bonnet 3V3 to GND is not a short. Fix anything that fails before going on.

First power, bonnet still off the Pi: plug in the 15 W supply through the USB-C meter. At the bonnet's header, pins 2 and 4 read 4.9 to 5.1 V, the LED and BTN pins read under 1 V, and the 3V3 pins read 0 V. Unplug, press the bonnet onto the Pi's header, and stick the amp flat on top of the bonnet over the middle of the Pi with a square of 1 mm foam tape.

Close the head: bring the lower shell up under the upper so the lip seats all round with no wire across it, then drive 4 x M3 x 8 up through the wells in the lower shell into the inserts. Check the shutter nub still slides.

Close the base: fit the bottom plate with 6 x M3 x 8 up through its counterbored holes, with no wire under the lip. Stick the four rubber feet into their pockets. Write the unit number in the engraved UNIT NO. field with the paint marker.

Pose: hold the base down on the desk with one hand and bend the gooseneck with the other (the unit tips at about 1 to 2 N at the head otherwise) to the design pose: lens 220 mm above the desk and 120 mm in front of the arm root, head nose-down about 15 deg, long side parallel to the base's front edge.

Per-unit software: boot, then set the hostname to ponder-NN (`sudo raspi-config nonint do_hostname ponder-NN`), write the backend URL and this unit's token into /etc/ponder/device.conf, record the Wi-Fi MAC (`cat /sys/class/net/wlan0/address`) for IT, turn on the overlay file system (`sudo raspi-config nonint do_overlayfs 0`) and reboot.

Unit test sheet (every unit; write each result in the build log). Load: run a 10 minute soak with the camera streaming (`rpicam-vid -t 600000 --nopreview -o /dev/null`), a tone through the speaker (`speaker-test -c 2 -t sine -f 440`) and the light bar white; every minute read `vcgencmd measure_temp` and `vcgencmd get_throttled`, and measure 5V at the bonnet with the meter. Pass: under 80 C, get_throttled 0x0 at the end, 5V at 4.75 V or more (if it dips, lower the volume or brightness cap). Light bar: a sweep script lights each of the 8 pixels red, green, blue and white in turn, at idle and during the soak. Page: put a Letter test page with pencil text in all four corners and the middle in front of the base, open the shutter, take `rpicam-still --lens-position 3.6 -o test.jpg`, copy it off with `scp`, and read every corner at full resolution. Closed shutter: the image is black. Mics: record 5 s of stereo while talking (`arecord -c 2 -r 48000 -f S32_LE -d 5 t.wav`), then compare `sox t.wav -n remix 1 stat` and `remix 2 stat`: both channels carry the voice, within about 6 dB. Speak at a normal voice from 60 cm and check it is clearly heard on playback. On MUTE: the red light is on, both channels are silent, and GPIO24 reads high (`pinctrl get 24`). Speaker: at the volume cap a spoken prompt is clear from 60 cm. Lights and button: `pinctrl set 25 op dh` lights the green light; after `pinctrl set 23 ip pu`, `pinctrl get 23` reads lo while the talk button is held. Wi-Fi: `iw dev wlan0 link` shows the school network with the head closed.

First article only, after its test sheet passes: tip test, pressing down on the head and pushing it sideways at head height with a luggage scale (the checks say it tips at about 3.7 N down and 1.2 to 2.4 N at head height; record what it takes). Drop test: drop the unit from desk height (760 mm) onto the head, then onto a base corner, then run the test sheet again. Record any crack, loose part or failed test, and fix the design before order B.

Close the shutter, put the unit in its box with its supply (use only the supplied adapter, as the base says), and record the unit number, SD card, Wi-Fi MAC, test results and date in the build log. Tell the teacher to hold the base when moving the arm.

lines.notes: Substitute for Adafruit 3220, which is out of stock. Same DPDT ON-ON function with solder lugs, but a 1/4-40 bushing: the head's toggle hole is 6.5 mm (was 6 mm) and the CAD envelope for the body is 13.2 x 13.2 mm (was 13.1 x 12.6). designMd:
# Ponder: design

**Request:** a screenless desk tutor for kids 6 to 14. It looks down at the homework, listens, and talks back; a cloud
model does the thinking. 20 units for a school pilot, US, wall power. No budget was given, so none is set.

**What it is:** a document camera crossed with a voice kit. A weighted base (150 x 100 x 40 mm) holds the speaker, a
talk button, a status light bar and the power input. A 15 in lamp gooseneck rises from it and holds a head pod
(116 x 45 x 34 mm) with its lens about 220 mm above the desk and 120 mm in front of the arm root, nose down 15 deg.
The head holds the computer, the camera, two microphones, the amplifier, the mute switch and the two privacy lights.
The whole unit weighs about 1,075 g. Every number lives in `design.json` → `params`; the CAD and the checks read
them from there.

## Reference designs

- **Audio: Google AIY Voice Kit V1 (Voice HAT).** Two I2S MEMS mics (ICS-43432) and a MAX98357A amp on the Pi's I2S
  pins, amp shutdown on GPIO16, button on GPIO23, driven by the stock `googlevoicehat-soundcard` overlay. Ponder
  rebuilds that circuit from breakouts. [Voice Kit docs](https://aiyprojects.readthedocs.io/en/latest/voice.html),
  [schematic](https://github.com/google/aiyprojects-raspbian/blob/aiyprojects/schematics/voice_hat/voice_hat.pdf),
  [pinout](https://pinout.xyz/pinout/voice_hat).
- **Camera and privacy light: Google AIY Vision Kit.** A Pi Zero with a camera on a short flex cable and a privacy
  LED beside the lens. [Vision Kit](https://aiyprojects.withgoogle.com/vision/).
- **Mic and amp wiring:** Adafruit's guides for the
  [SPH0645 mic on a Pi](https://learn.adafruit.com/adafruit-i2s-mems-microphone-breakout/raspberry-pi-wiring-test)
  and the [MAX98357A on a Pi](https://learn.adafruit.com/adafruit-max98357-i2s-class-d-mono-amp/raspberry-pi-wiring).
- **Status lights:** Adafruit's [NeoPixels on Raspberry Pi](https://learn.adafruit.com/neopixels-on-raspberry-pi/raspberry-pi-wiring)
  (GPIO10, with the 1N4001 trick so 3.3 V data drives 5 V pixels) and the
  [rpi_ws281x README](https://github.com/jgarff/rpi_ws281x) for `core_freq=250` on the Pi 3 family.
- **Arm and base: a USB document camera** such as the [IPEVO V4K](https://us.ipevo.com/pages/v4k-specs), built here
  from standard 1/8 IPS lamp parts (hollow gooseneck, couplings, nipples, nuts) with steel discs on the lamp pipe.
  [Grand Brass goosenecks](https://grandbrass.com/pipe/goose-neck-pipe/).

`reference/reference.json` turns these into the answer key the run is scored against.

## Stack

- Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W with header (SC0721), Raspberry Pi OS Lite 64-bit on a 32 GB Class 10 card.
- Camera Module 3 Wide (SC0874): IMX708, 102 x 67 deg
  ([product brief](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/camera/camera-module-3-product-brief.pdf)), on the 38 mm
  Standard-Mini cable from the official Pi Zero case kit (Adafruit 3446).
- 2 x SPH0645 I2S mic breakouts, MAX98357A I2S amp breakout, 40 mm 4 ohm 3 W speaker (PUI AS04004PR-R).
- NeoPixel stick (8 pixels), 16 mm green talk button, a miniature DPDT on-on toggle for mute (Jameco 66-1205),
  green and red 5 mm LEDs.
- Perma-Proto Bonnet Mini on the Pi (all head wiring), a quarter Perma-Proto in the base (power split).
- Raspberry Pi 15 W USB-C supply (5.1 V, 3 A) into a USB-C breakout in the base.
- Six prints: base top, base bottom, head upper, head lower and lens shutter in PA12 (MJF), and a light-bar
  diffuser in natural PETG, all from one print service.

## How the blocks connect

**Why the computer is in the head.** The camera's flat cable can't go through a lamp gooseneck. With the Pi beside
the camera, only round wires go through the arm. The camera cable stays in the head: the path between the two
connectors is about 32 mm, so the 38 mm cable makes one short loop.

**The arm harness** is one 10-wire 28 AWG silicone ribbon, 690 mm: 1-3 5V, 4 GND, 5 SPK+, 6 SPK-, 7 GND, 8 LED
data, 9 GND, 10 BTN. A ground sits between the unfiltered speaker pair and the light-bar data, and another between
the data and the button. The LED data reaches the stick through 440 ohm; the button is debounced in software.

**Inside the head.** The lower shell carries the camera on four pins over the lens window, the lens shutter in a track
under it, and the Pi on four posts with 6 mm deep M2.5 insert holes. The bonnet sits on the Pi, and the amp lies flat
on top of the bonnet. The upper shell carries the mics in pockets behind their ports, the two lights, the mute toggle
in the camera end (with MUTE moulded under it), and the nipple that joins the head to the arm. The toggle body sits
0.8 mm above the camera board, so the camera can't lift off its pins far even if the glue lets go. Four M3 screws
close the head from below.

**Arm and ballast.** At the base the coupling sits in a seat on a 2 mm collar. A 1-3/4 in nipple, screwed 8 mm into
it, goes down through the top shell, a printed column and two 3 in x 1/4 in steel discs (Wagner D143-.44CH, 213 g
each), and a nut under the discs clamps the stack. The pipe's lower end stays 3.9 mm above the harness groove, so the
ten wires can turn out under it. The arm holes are 11 mm for a 10.29 mm pipe. The gooseneck leaves the base pointing
up and turns about 165 deg into the head's top coupling: at a 40 mm bend radius that needs about 335 mm, so the 15 in
(381 mm) gooseneck is used. The 12 in one is too short.

**Power.** USB-C → 120 mm of 22 AWG → base protoboard → 3 x 5 V up the arm to the bonnet's 5 V rail. The check now
models the supply at its -5 % load-regulation limit, the amp's sine-wave peaks, the USB-C contacts and the base feed.
Typical use (amp capped at 2.5 W, light bar at 50 %) gives 4.77 V at the head, just above the 4.75 V USB low limit.
The worst case (supply at 4.84 V, full volume, light bar white) gives 4.31 V, so the check is a flag: measure 5 V at
the bonnet on every unit, and lower the caps if it dips. The Pi figure (635 mA) is a
[measured peak](https://www.cnx-software.com/2021/12/09/raspberry-pi-zero-2-w-power-consumption/); the amp's 85 %
efficiency into 4 ohm is an estimate (the datasheet gives 92 % only for 8 ohm at 1 W); the camera's 250 mA is an
allowance. Adafruit gives no current rating for the USB-C breakout, so the 3 A input figure is flagged too.

**Audio.** I2S on GPIO18-21 with the Pi as master. Both mics share the clocks (through 1 k resistors) and one data
line, left and right picked by SEL. The amp shares the clocks and takes GPIO21. Its SD pin is driven at 3.3 V, which
selects the left channel, so the client plays mono. An ALSA softvol control caps it at 2.5 W, under the speaker's 3 W
rating. The grille is 35.6 mm, the speaker's baffle opening.

**Lights and button.** The light bar is on SPI0 MOSI (GPIO10), which keeps it off the I2S pins. The Zero 2 W has the
Pi 3's SoC, whose SPI clock follows the core clock, so config.txt sets `core_freq=250`. Talk button on GPIO23, mute
sense on GPIO24, camera light on GPIO25 (about 10 mA), amp shutdown on GPIO16.

## Privacy, in plain terms

- **Mic mute is hardware.** Pole 2 of the toggle opens the mics' data wire and ties the Pi's input to ground, so no
  audio can reach the Pi. That cut is what makes the mute real. Pole 1 disconnects the mics' 3.3 V and lights the red
  light, so the light is on exactly when the mics are cut; the mic supply is left floating, and the clocks can part-power
  the mics through their 1 k resistors, which is why the data cut matters. Software can read the switch (GPIO24) but
  can't undo it. It covers the built-in mics only, not a Bluetooth headset's, so the client must not use one.
- **The camera light is software, by choice.** The green light is on GPIO25, and the client turns it on before it
  starts the camera. A hardware light is possible without a custom PCB: the camera connector carries the camera's
  power-enable line (CAM_GPIO0 on the Zero 2 W schematic), which could drive the LED through a transistor breakout.
  That is not in this build. The hardware guarantee is the printed lens shutter: closed means the sensor sees nothing.
- **No local storage is a configured promise.** Stock Raspberry Pi OS writes swap, logs and temp files to the card.
  The golden image turns off swap on the card, keeps the journal in RAM, puts /tmp in RAM and turns on the overlay
  file system, so nothing the client handles survives a reboot. Check it with `swapon --show`, `findmnt /tmp` and
  `raspi-config`'s overlay status.

## Software

The Ponder device client does not exist yet; the B0tes/ponder-tutor repo holds the web app only. The build plan sets
up one golden SD card (OS, config.txt, packages, ALSA config, storage settings) and copies it to all 21 cards. Each
unit then gets its hostname, its backend token in /etc/ponder/device.conf and the overlay file system, and its Wi-Fi
MAC is logged for the school's IT staff. The client still has to be written to this spec: push-to-talk on GPIO23 with
software debounce, mute from GPIO24, the camera light on GPIO25 around every capture, the light bar on SPI at no more
than 50 %, mono playback, a fixed lens position (3.6 dioptres to start), no headset microphone, frames and audio in
RAM only.

The Zero 2 W has 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi only, and many school networks need WPA2-Enterprise logins or MAC registration, so the
plan asks the school's IT staff first.

## Handling and stability

At 1,075 g the unit stands with the head over the page (26 mm inside the front feet). It is easy to tip on purpose:
pressing down on the head tips it at about 3.7 N, and a push at head height at 1.2 to 2.4 N. Bending a gooseneck
takes more force than that, so the base must be held with the other hand while the arm is adjusted. With the arm
pulled straight out the unit falls over. More steel does not fit under the junction board; a wider or deeper base,
or the arm root further back, would fix it in the next version. For the pilot this is accepted and the teachers are
told. The first unit gets a tip test and a drop test before the other units are ordered.

## What changed in review

- **Harness exit at the arm root.** The pipe end used to sit 0.65 to 1.65 mm above the groove floor, which would crush
  the wires. A collar under the coupling, 8 mm disc ribs, a deeper groove and an 8 mm thread engagement now leave
  3.9 mm (the check asks for 3.4).
- **Arm holes 11 mm** (were 10 mm, under the real 10.29 mm pipe OD).
- **15 in gooseneck** instead of 12 in (the 165 deg turn needs about 335 mm). It is also cheaper.
- **38 mm camera cable** instead of 200 mm (there was nowhere to stow 170 mm of spare flat cable).
- **M2.5 holes 2 mm deeper**, with a new check, so the Pi screws can't bottom out.
- **Junction board pins are heat-staked**, the solder side and the disc both get Kapton, the USB-C breakout is glued
  into its cradle, and the light-bar stick is glued into its frame.
- **Mouldings:** MUTE under the toggle, and "use only the supplied 5.1V 3A USB-C adapter" with a unit-number field
  under the base.
- **Order:** spares on the lines that break or get lost, a 22 AWG hook-up wire set for the power runs, pack counts in
  the order list, and a two-phase order (below). The shutter now goes to the same print service as the head lower it
  slides in.

## Cost

As one order, the quote is **$5,371.43 for 20 units, $268.57 each**, spares included. That is about $2,948 of
electronics, $786 of arm, ballast and fasteners, $1,349 of prints and $287 of shipping, 16.1 % above the middle of the
reference band ($4,250 to $5,000). The biggest lines are the cameras ($700), the base-top prints ($546), the Pi kits
($460), the SD cards ($419) and the goosenecks ($383).

The build plan orders in two phases instead: **order A ($822.65)** builds 2 units to measure, and **order B
($4,699.52)** buys the rest and the spares once they pass. Together that is $5,522.17, $150.74 more than one order,
mostly a second round of shipping. Order A buys all 20 speakers, because Master Electronics sells them in twenties.

Not in either total:

- **Import duty on the Pi kits.** The only Zero 2 W with header in stock is Seeed's Basic Kit, shipped from China
  under DAP terms. Seeed's customs page cites a 45 % base tariff on dev boards: about $207 if it applies.
- **Mouser tariffs and insurance.** A reviewer read an 8 % tariff note on the camera's Mouser page (about $56); the
  Mouser pages would not load here to confirm it. Insurance adds about $7.
- **The print rate is unverified.** Craftcloud's $0.30/cm3 with a $6 minimum a part is not on its site; upload the
  STLs for a real quote. The diffuser and shutter cost $132 each only because of that minimum.
- Consumables, tools, sales tax, and DHL transit and customs time for the Seeed order.

Shipping is an estimate for most shops (see `catalog.json` → `_shippingBasis`).

## Check on the first unit

Assembly step 1 lists every item with its pass rule; order B waits until they all pass. The main unknowns are the
gooseneck (hollow, thread gender, bore, mass, bend radius and rigid end lengths are not published), the Camera
Module 3 hole positions (read from an unlabelled drawing), the toggle size and contact material, the junction board
holes, the USB-C socket height, the mic ports, the M3 insert hole, the bonnet header's gender and the Seeed kit's
contents, the voltage at the head under load, the Wi-Fi signal inside the head next to the steel nut, and the drop
and tip tests.

## Still to decide

Whether the pilot units need the CPSIA Children's Product Certificate and FCC Part 15B steps before they go to a
school. A printed tracking label with the module's FCC ID is still to be designed. The rubber feet can be peeled off
and are small enough to swallow; that matters only for younger siblings, but a moulded foot would remove it.

Harness LED wire (8) through two 220 ohm in series to the stick's DIN, as close to the stick as the wire allows; BTN (10) to the other button leg; SPK+ and SPK- (5, 6) to the speaker. Trim every lead flush on the solder side and cover that side with Kapton.
26. Press the junction board onto its two posts and heat-stake the pins: touch each pin tip with the flat of the iron until it mushrooms over the hole. Then slide the discs and the nut up the wires onto the nipple and run the nut up tight with the wrench, so coupling, shell, column and discs clamp together; hold the gooseneck with the strap wrench so it doesn't twist. The Kapton face of the top disc now sits about 2.8 mm under the board's Kapton-covered solder side.
27. Set the USB-C breakout in the cradle on the bottom plate with its socket in the back-wall opening and fix it with hot glue on the cradle walls, so plugging in can't move it. Lay the harness tail in the groove under the nipple and out through the gap in the disc ring.
28. Before first power, with the bonnet unplugged from the Pi and no supply connected, beep with the meter: harness 5V to GND at the bonnet is not a short (the reading climbs as the capacitors charge); the BTN and LED wires show no continuity to 5V; BTN shows continuity to GND only while the talk button is held; bonnet 3V3 to GND is not a short. Fix anything that fails before going on.
29. First power, bonnet still off the Pi: plug in the 15 W supply through the USB-C meter. At the bonnet's header, pins 2 and 4 read 4.9 to 5.1 V, the LED and BTN pins read under 1 V, and the 3V3 pins read 0 V. Unplug, press the bonnet onto the Pi's header, and stick the amp flat on top of the bonnet over the middle of the Pi with a square of 1 mm foam tape.
30. Close the head: bring the lower shell up under the upper so the lip seats all round with no wire across it, then drive 4 x M3 x 8 up through the wells in the lower shell into the inserts. Check the shutter nub still slides.
31. Close the base: fit the bottom plate with 6 x M3 x 8 up through its counterbored holes, with no wire under the lip. Stick the four rubber feet into their pockets. Write the unit number in the engraved UNIT NO. field with the paint marker.
32. Pose: hold the base down on the desk with one hand and bend the gooseneck with the other (the unit tips at about 1 to 2 N at the head otherwise) to the design pose: lens 220 mm above the desk and 120 mm in front of the arm root, head nose-down about 15 deg, long side parallel to the base's front edge.
33. Per-unit software: boot, then set the hostname to ponder-NN (`sudo raspi-config nonint do_hostname ponder-NN`), write the backend URL and this unit's token into /etc/ponder/device.conf, record the Wi-Fi MAC (`cat /sys/class/net/wlan0/address`) for IT, turn on the overlay file system (`sudo raspi-config nonint do_overlayfs 0`) and reboot.
34. Unit test sheet (every unit; write each result in the build log). Load: run a 10 minute soak with the camera streaming (`rpicam-vid -t 600000 --nopreview -o /dev/null`), a tone through the speaker (`speaker-test -c 2 -t sine -f 440`) and the light bar white; every minute read `vcgencmd measure_temp` and `vcgencmd get_throttled`, and measure 5V at the bonnet with the meter. Pass: under 80 C, get_throttled 0x0 at the end, 5V at 4.75 V or more (if it dips, lower the volume or brightness cap). Light bar: a sweep script lights each of the 8 pixels red, green, blue and white in turn, at idle and during the soak. Page: put a Letter test page with pencil text in all four corners and the middle in front of the base, open the shutter, take `rpicam-still --lens-position 3.6 -o test.jpg`, copy it off with `scp`, and read every corner at full resolution. Closed shutter: the image is black. Mics: record 5 s of stereo while talking (`arecord -c 2 -r 48000 -f S32_LE -d 5 t.wav`), then compare `sox t.wav -n remix 1 stat` and `remix 2 stat`: both channels carry the voice, within about 6 dB. Speak at a normal voice from 60 cm and check it is clearly heard on playback. On MUTE: the red light is on, both channels are silent, and GPIO24 reads high (`pinctrl get 24`). Speaker: at the volume cap a spoken prompt is clear from 60 cm. Lights and button: `pinctrl set 25 op dh` lights the green light; after `pinctrl set 23 ip pu`, `pinctrl get 23` reads lo while the talk button is held. Wi-Fi: `iw dev wlan0 link` shows the school network with the head closed.
35. First article only, after its test sheet passes: tip test, pressing down on the head and pushing it sideways at head height with a luggage scale (the checks say it tips at about 3.7 N down and 1.2 to 2.4 N at head height; record what it takes). Drop test: drop the unit from desk height (760 mm) onto the head, then onto a base corner, then run the test sheet again. Record any crack, loose part or failed test, and fix the design before order B.
36. Close the shutter, put the unit in its box with its supply (use only the supplied adapter, as the base says), and record the unit number, SD card, Wi-Fi MAC, test results and date in the build log. Tell the teacher to hold the base when moving the arm.
